newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian PM pledges tough economic package.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian PM pledges tough economic package.

text.p: Bulgarian Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said on Monday the government planned a package of measures to stabilise the economy and he hoped parliament could vote on introduction of a currency board regime on January 2.

Videnov told a news conference the Socialist government's programme for 1997 and 1998 included financial stabilisation and structural reform measures which he said would bring stable growth in the last two years of his mandate.
"I think by December 31 we will manage to debate and take decisions on the introduction of a currency board so parliament can approve the draft proposal on January 2," Videnov said.
He said the cabinet planned to submit a draft 1997 budget by the end of December and parliament would cancel its Christmas recess if necessary to get the measures through.

He said the cabinet would accompany the currency board with a package of structural reform measures which would include a programme for the second stage of the mass privatisation voucher scheme and some big privatisation deals.
"If such a package is not approved by parliament, our government will have to resign," he said.

A currency board is a form of fixed exchange rate regime which requires the government to match levs in circulation and commercial banks' reserves at the central bank with foreign currency and gold reserves.

The system was recommended to Bulgaria by the International Monetary Fund whose mission was in Sofia on Monday to discuss the government's plans, which, if bold enough, should allow the Fund to resume much needed financial assistance. The government has been slow to deliver on previous promises of structural reform but economists warn that a lev peg alone will not solve Bulgaria's economic problems. They say it must be accompanied by a serious commitment to measures delayed in the seven years since the end of one-party rule.

The currency board mechanism removes political pressure on the central bank to print money. Videnov said increased austerity would affect all budget programmes, but the first priority would be payment of foreign and domestic debt, followed by social security for the poor and unemployed.

He dismissed recent sharp falls in the lev as speculation and said banks holding long foreign exchange positions risked losing money because a currency board would be introduced in conjunction with a higher level for the lev, which closed at 515-530 on Monday.
"Everyone's speculating, but there are no deals," he said of the interbank foreign exchange market. "Any level below 300-350 is unreasonable."
Videnov said the government would finalise the sale of a 60 percent stake in chemical firm Sodi Devnya, Bulgaria's biggest privatisation to date, by the end of the week.
The government is in talks with U.S. firm General Chemical Inc which has offered $160 million for the stake.

Videnov said the government should negotiate to sell some pharmaceutical plants and other enterprises such as fork lift truck producers, and finalise the planned sale of a 25 percent stake in Bulgarian Telecommunications Company.

Videnov said that he would propose radical changes in the government at a Socialist party congress on December 21 and 22, and accused the opposition of trying to make political capital out of the economic crisis.
